description: We are a group of school students using our skills and creativity to build tools that help the newer generation learn.
summary:
Unibot is a free browser game that lets kids fly their own 30-day mission to Mars. Players command a small spaceship with the help of MOTHER, a friendly AI ship computer. They keep power, air, water and food running, shelter from a solar storm, land on Mars, and explore a large map in a rover. On Mars they drill rock cores, set down a seismometer, clean solar panels, fix a weather station, rescue a lost helicopter, scan rocks with a laser microscope and fly a Mars helicopter to take photos from the sky.

Every mission ends with a real fact from NASA missions, with a link to learn more, so kids learn real science while they play. Friends can join the same ship (up to 4 players) with a room code.

Space exploration often feels far away and hard to understand for children. Unibot turns it into something they can do with their own hands: plan, make choices, solve problems and work as a team, just like a real crew. It runs in any browser, with no install or account, so any school or home can use it.
details:
Unibot is a top-down pixel-art game that runs in the web browser on computers and touch devices. A mission starts with a 3 to 5-day trip to Mars (Easy, Medium or Hard). Players walk through the ship’s rooms, use stations, and react to events such as a solar storm. After landing, Mars becomes a large explorable map: players drive a rover with a limited battery, avoid craters and deep sand, find shiny rocks, and complete science jobs shown as step lists. Short first-person scenes show each job through the astronaut’s helmet, and a laser microscope lets players scan rocks and read their spectrum.

MOTHER, the ship’s AI computer, guides players and answers typed questions in simple, kid-safe language. Her answers are grounded in the game’s 38 real mission facts, which never repeat until all have been seen. Co-op multiplayer lets up to 4 friends share one ship, take turns at the controls and chat with filtered quick phrases.

Benefits: it is free, needs no download or account, saves progress automatically, and works on low-cost devices. The intended impact is to spark curiosity about Mars exploration and teach how astronauts manage resources, why space weather matters, and how rovers, drills, seismometers and helicopters do real science.

Tools: TypeScript, Phaser 3 and Vite for the game; all art and sound effects are generated in code. It is hosted on Cloudflare Workers, with Durable Objects for multiplayer rooms and Workers AI for MOTHER’s answers. AI coding assistance (Claude) helped write the code.

Creativity and design factors: we chose pixel art and short missions to suit young players, added difficulty levels, kept controls to a few keys or a touch pad, filtered chat and AI answers for child safety, collect no personal data, and gave every fact a link to its source (NASA pages for all but one).
